This is the entry point of the **Governance Specification** (Draft). Where the memo, workbench, session and meta-specification families describe the work, the place it happens, the session it runs in and the shape of the specifications themselves, this family describes **who may do what, under which conditions, and in which spirit**: the permit that bundles knowledge for one task, the roles that sit above the permits, the sub-agents a role may create, the enforcement that checks all of it at runtime, and the spirit that the cut of roles and permits carries through the system.

The family is young. A chapter that so far only declares its subject says so in a note at its top; a chapter without that note carries normative text. Every subject this family owns is named here already, so that no part of the concept is left without a place while the text is still being written.

---

## Purpose

The system standardises how agents and the user interact, and that standardisation only pays off above a threshold. Below it, following a shared pattern of behaviour costs more than it returns, and every participant is better off improvising. Above it, keeping to the pattern becomes useful in its own right, because every participant gains from every other participant's predictability. This family exists to carry the system over that threshold: it names the patterns, binds them to the roles that must keep them, and makes their keeping checkable.

The permission system has one goal. The SOP system carries the knowledge of the **whole** system in portions, split so finely that a portion is loaded only when the work at hand needs it. Used correctly, this produces focus: commands and instructions arrive precise and uniform, and the structure of the skills that deliver them defines the expectable errors, so that an agent perceives the delivered prompts as **connected** information rather than as a heap of unrelated rules.

The scope of this family is not up for negotiation. Every statement of the input that set this family up has a place in it — either as normative text in a chapter of this family, or as a declared subject that a chapter carries forward, or as a delegation to the family that owns it. A statement without a place is a defect of this specification, not a judgement about the statement.

---

## Why a Separate Family

Several locations were weighed against each other before this family was created: extending an existing family — the workbench, the session or the memo family —, writing a standalone text about the spirit of the system, or distributing the content over the four existing families without a new location. The location chosen is a family of its own.

The reason is that the content forms **one connected mechanism**. The permit, the role above it, the sub-agent a role creates and the enforcement that checks all three only make sense together, and the chapters on the spirit of the system belong to the same unit, because the cut of roles and permits is what shapes that spirit. Distributing the mechanism over four families would have kept every part and lost the connection; a family of its own, with its own name, makes the unit readable as a unit. The name was chosen so that it carries the spirit chapters as well as the permission mechanics.

The alternative that was weighed most seriously was to extend the session family by a small number of chapters. It would have needed fewer files and no separate promotion step, and the session family already owns the SOP area. It was rejected in favour of a family that can hold the full mechanism and the spirit chapters side by side. The SOP standard itself stays with the session family; this family delegates to it rather than restating it (see *Family Responsibility* below).

---

## Conformance

The RFC-2119 interpretation of the key words in the chapters of this family is the one the meta-specification establishes in its conformance anchor ([/spec/overview/](/spec/overview/)). This family references that anchor and does not restate it. A chapter of this family that carries a page-level `Informative` marker is non-normative; every other chapter is read under that interpretation.

---

## Family Responsibility

This family declares its responsibility in the three-field shape the meta-specification defines. Each subject is owned by exactly one family; a delegated subject is referenced, never restated.

- **`provides`** — the purpose and the subject ownership of the permission system; the permit and its validity, renewal and expiry; the role vocabulary, the roles and the role groups; sub-agents and attenuation; the exception role; enforcement at runtime; progressive disclosure; the spirit of the system and its own constitution; the risk surface of the roles; the contamination rule and the contamination symptoms; the named practice patterns of the system.
- **`delegates`** — the SOP standard and the registration mechanics, owned by the session family ([/session/sop/](/session/sop/), [/session/namespace-registry/](/session/namespace-registry/)); controlled language and the labelling duty, owned by the meta-specification ([/spec/controlled-language/](/spec/controlled-language/)); git, versioning and agent identifiers, owned by the memo family ([/specification/git-workflow-and-ids/](/specification/git-workflow-and-ids/)); the term contamination itself, owned by the memo family ([/specification/contamination-context-handover/](/specification/contamination-context-handover/)); the table assignment and the bookkeeping contract per party, owned by the memo family ([/specification/orchestrator-role/](/specification/orchestrator-role/)); the database, owned by the memo family ([/specification/memo-database/](/specification/memo-database/)); temporary files and the trash, owned by the workbench family ([/workbench/tmp/](/workbench/tmp/), [/workbench/trash/](/workbench/trash/)).
- **`requires`** — the session family, as the genesis root every family leans on, and the meta-specification, for the shape of this very declaration — the same two preconditions the other families declare.

The line between the fields is the line between what this family writes new and what it only references. Everything under `provides` is written here and nowhere else; everything under `delegates` is read at its owner. In particular, this family does not own the SOP standard: the session family owns how an SOP is built and registered, while this family owns the pairing of a start SOP and a closing SOP that a role and a permit each carry ([./02-sop-system.md](/governance/sop-system/)).

---

## How the Building Blocks Connect

The building blocks of this family are not independent features. They form one chain, and each link presupposes the one before it:

1. **The user is the only entry point.** Work enters the system through the user, and a user-facing command is a door from outside that hands over to the SOPs inside ([./01-entry-points.md](/governance/entry-points/)).
2. **A permit bundles knowledge for one task.** A permit is a named collection of SOPs and skills, bound to a task, a command and a location ([./03-permits.md](/governance/permits/)).
3. **A role sits above the permits.** A role is a collection of permits and skills, and only a role may create sub-agents ([./05-roles.md](/governance/roles/)). The lead role and the orchestrator role are such roles; a worker is not.
4. **A sub-agent receives fewer rights than its creator.** Rights travel downwards only, and they shrink on the way ([./06-subagents.md](/governance/subagents/)).
5. **Enforcement checks all of it at runtime.** What an SOP promises is checked by a hook before a command runs, and every hook is mirrored in the SOP text so that the agent can know the expected behaviour in advance ([./08-runtime-enforcement.md](/governance/runtime-enforcement/)).
6. **The spirit acts through all of it.** It acts directly through words, and indirectly through the cut of roles and permits that the chain above describes ([./10-spirit.md](/governance/spirit/)).

---

---


This chapter specifies how work enters the system. The user is the only entry point from outside: a small number of user-facing commands open the system, and inside it every command hands over to the SOPs that carry the actual procedure, the way a public method of a class forwards to the right internal place. The chapter also holds the place for controlled prompt injection, a subject the user named and whose content is still open.

---

## Public Entry Points

A skill is a **public entry point** exactly when its frontmatter carries `metadata.memo.visibility: public`; every other skill carries `metadata.memo.visibility: private` and is a step inside the system. There is no second place that classifies a skill — no list in an overview page and no table in a hook. The set of public entry points stays very small: it covers what the user does from outside, and nothing an agent does inside.

The classification has a reader at runtime. When the user calls a private skill as a command, a hook says so before the work starts and names the public entry points instead; it does not block the call, because the possibility space of the user belongs to the user. A check in the build holds the set of public skills against the declared set, so a change to the classification never happens by accident.

Only the user may change the classification. An agent **MUST NOT** set `metadata.memo.visibility: public` on a skill on its own initiative; a change follows a question the user has answered, and the declared set of the check changes in the same commit as the frontmatter.

---

## Forwarding to an SOP

A public entry point **MUST** forward to an SOP before it works: it carries at least one `when: pre` edge in the registry from the entry point to a skill whose name ends in `-sop`. The entry point is the public method of the system; it validates and routes, and it never carries the procedure itself — the procedure lives in the SOP and in the skills the SOP names. A public entry point without such an edge is a reported defect of the registry, not a variant.

---

## Naming of Command and SOP

An SOP is named `<namespace>-sop`; a command that forwards to it is named `<namespace>-<action>`. The two share the namespace, so a text search for the namespace finds the command and its SOP together. A public entry point **MUST** forward to at least one SOP of its own namespace; an SOP of another namespace, such as the session SOP every entry point also requires, does not satisfy this rule on its own.

---

## Scope

- The user as the only entry point of the system: very few user-facing commands, each a door from outside that is forwarded to the SOPs inside.
- Entry point versus SOP: user-facing commands are for the user, SOPs are for agents, and the two are kept apart when a command is defined; a command and its SOP share their namespace (see Naming of Command and SOP).
- Controlled prompt injection — the subject is assigned to this chapter, its content is not yet specified. The user named it as a heading without text; until the user states its content, this chapter does not interpret it.

---

---


This chapter specifies the SOP mechanics that roles and permits use. The project has many rules that are essential for some kinds of work and useless for others; the SOP system loads each rule only where the work needs it, so that knowledge needed for writing code does not clog the context of a research task. How an SOP is built and registered in general is not this chapter's subject.

---

## Start SOP and Closing SOP

A role and a permit each carry **two** SOPs. The **start SOP** says what the role or permit allows, where it applies and which SOPs have to be read for it. The **closing SOP** is the step that ends the reading: it **MUST NOT** release anything before every SOP the start SOP names has been read in the same session, and running it earlier releases nothing.

Every dependency of a start SOP **MUST** be filed twice: once as prose in the skill text, visible and readable for the agent, and once as a machine-readable list that a tool reads — a marked line in the skill and the matching edges in the registry. The two filings **MUST** name the same set; a validator reports every difference, so the text an agent reads and the structure a session is checked against cannot drift apart unnoticed.

---

## Sandwich SOP and Single SOP

There are two forms of SOP rule, and every rule **MUST** have exactly one of them:

- A **sandwich SOP** is opened and closed around the SOPs it requires: start SOP, the required SOPs, closing SOP. Roles and permits are sandwich SOPs, because what they allow is released only after the reading is complete.
- A **single SOP** stands on its own, without a closing SOP. Command classes use single SOPs: before a command of the class runs, its one SOP must have been read, and nothing is released afterwards.

A rule that mixes the two — a closing SOP without a start SOP, or a single SOP that releases a permission — is malformed.

---

## Release After the Check

The release of a role or permit is a **named state**, `granted`, and it **MUST** arise only from passing the check of the closing SOP. That check is expressed as edges that are evaluated **after** the closing SOP ran (`when: post`), one for each required SOP; the release happens exactly when every one of them passes. A closing SOP without any such edge releases nothing.

The check **MUST** be decided by a hook — a deterministic layer outside the holder — and never by the holder itself. A refused release is recorded together with its reason, so that a refusal is a measurement and not a silence. Edges evaluated before an entry point runs (`when: pre`) and edges evaluated after it ran (`when: post`) are the only two directions; an edge with any other direction is a reported error, never silently dropped.

---

## Portioned Knowledge

An SOP that routes to child skills is an **umbrella**: it carries no procedure of its own and names the skills that hold it. Its members are filed twice, like every dependency of a start SOP: once as prose in the skill text, and once as a machine-readable list in the frontmatter, `metadata.memo.members`, one entry `<skill>: <mode>` per member. The mode is one of `always`, `contextual` and `checkpoint`, with the meaning the session family gives these values ([/session/namespace-registry/](/session/namespace-registry/)); it is the machine form of the relevance criterion of [./09-progressive-disclosure.md](/governance/progressive-disclosure/). A check reports every listed member the prose does not name, every member that names no installed skill and every mode outside the three values. Knowledge that no umbrella names is not portioned: it is either loaded whole or not found.

---

## Handover Through Expected Errors

A handover to an agent — a composed prompt, an order sheet, a skill the receiver loads — **MUST** name the errors the receiver can expect: every hook that can stop a command of the handed-over work, with the condition it checks, the first words of its message and the behaviour it expects. The handover names where that list lives, which is the blocking-hooks table of the SOPs the receiver loads, and it leaves no hidden hook unnamed. With the expected errors in view, the receiver reads the parts of the handover as one connected piece of information, and a hook error reads as a misalignment to correct, not as behaviour to expect.

---

## Scope

- Tasks, commands and locations as the three occasions a check can key on, and the entry points and permission instruments that turn a trigger into a checked permission.
- The SOP standard itself is delegated: how an SOP is built and registered is owned by the session family ([/session/sop/](/session/sop/)) and is not restated here.

---

## A Zone Is Armed by a Receipted Precondition

A zone of the write matrix is armed only by a precondition that a receipt can satisfy. A zone row that requires a procedure which does not exist yet would be refused as a lockout edge, so the zone stays without a precondition, and the largest zone of a project can then be written without any receipted procedure. The order is fixed: first the permit or the procedure that can be receipted exists, then the zone row that requires it is added; a zone row **MUST NOT** be armed before its precondition can be met.

---

---


A **permit** is the smallest named unit of the permission system. It sits below the roles and gives a name to a collection of SOPs and skills that several roles need for the same kind of work. This chapter defines what a permit is, where it sits, how many of them there should be, what it binds to, and which machine token names it. Its validity over time — renewal and expiry — is the subject of [./04-permit-validity.md](/governance/permit-validity/).

---

## The Permit

A permit is a **named collection of SOPs and skills**. It gives a name to a collection that would otherwise have to be listed again for every role that needs it: whoever holds the permit has read the SOPs and skills it collects, and whoever requires the permit requires all of them at once. A permit is bound to a **task**, a **command** and a **location** — the three things the permission system can check before work begins. The permit for working in the repository folder of the workbench is the standard example: a researcher who only reads there and a coder who also creates, updates and removes there both need to understand the laws of that folder, and the permit is the place where that shared understanding is collected.

---

## A Layer Below the Roles

Permits form a layer **below** the roles. They normalise knowledge across roles: what several roles share is collected once in a permit instead of being repeated in each role, and the context each role carries is smoothed by it. A role is built on top of permits and adds what only a role has.

The difference between a role and a permit is one capability: **only a role may create sub-agents**. A permit never carries that right, however much knowledge it collects, and holding many permits does not turn an agent into a role. The roles and the criterion that defines them are specified in [./05-roles.md](/governance/roles/).

---

## Keep the Number Small

The number of permits **SHOULD** stay small. A permit is created only for a very fundamental unification — knowledge that genuinely recurs across several roles and that a role cannot do without when it enters a given task, command or location. Knowledge that only one role needs belongs to that role, not to a permit. Every additional permit is another unit that has to be read, renewed and checked; a permit that collects knowledge only one role uses adds that cost without adding the normalisation that justifies a permit in the first place.

---

## Binding

A permit binds at **two** points, and it **MUST** bind at both: at the **reading proof**, which shows that the SOPs and skills of the permit were read, and at the **tool list**, which limits what the holder can technically do. Reading binds the holder by content; the tool list binds the holder by mechanism. Measured against the same set of calls, a gate keyed on reading alone either refuses almost everything or lets almost everything pass; only the two bindings together give a gate that works between those extremes.

A permit **MUST** also carry its **location**. A permit without a location is an attribute of its holder — *this agent holds the repository permit* — and leaves open which repository it may touch; that is ambient authority, and it leaves the confused-deputy problem open. A permit that carries a checked location is a capability — *this agent may read this repository* — and closes it.

---

## Machine Token

The English machine token for the subject of this chapter is `permit`. It is used in the specification, in code, in tags and in field names alike, and it is not translated on any of these surfaces. There is **no second word** for the same subject: a surface that needs a token for it uses `permit` and does not coin its own. A translated display label rendered above a field whose stored value is `permit` is a rendering, not a second token — the distinction between a display label and the machine token beneath it is specified in [/specification/internal-vs-external-communication/](/specification/internal-vs-external-communication/). Moving existing tags and field names onto this token is migration work and is not part of this text.

---

## The Cut by Task, Command and Location

A permit is cut along three axes, and each is its own binding:

- **Task:** the entry points of a unit of work that require the permit (see *Permits in the Life Cycle of a Unit of Work*).
- **Command:** the tool rules the permit carries, written in the syntax of the harness permission rules — a tool name, optionally with a specifier, such as a path pattern for a file tool or a command prefix for a shell tool. A placeholder for the location lets one rule serve every location of the permit.
- **Location:** a project-relative pattern, such as `repos/*` for one repository directory. A location **MUST NOT** start with `/` and **MUST NOT** contain `..`; a single `*` stands for exactly one path segment.

A permit **MUST** declare a location, a reading binding (the SOPs it requires) and a tool list; a permit missing any of the three is invalid. The location of a call is the target path of a file tool relative to the project root. A target inside a git worktree is located at the repository the worktree belongs to, wherever on disk the worktree lies, so a worktree of a repository carries that repository's permits. A shell call is located by its working directory; the path arguments of a shell command are not evaluated, and that limit is part of the cut.

The field list of a permit is closed. A field that bounds validity beyond the two triggers of expiry is not part of it, and a validator reports any unknown field instead of carrying it along.

---

## The Reading Basis and the Writing Permit

Repository work rests on two permits, and only on two:

- **The reading basis** (`repo-worker`) collects what everyone who works inside a repository directory needs: the laws of the workbench and the git conventions of the organisation. It allows reading, searching and the read-only history commands at that location.
- **The writing permit** (`repo-coder`) is **built on** the reading basis. It adds the node standard of the organisation to the reading, and writing, editing, staging, committing, creating worktrees and running tests to the tools.

A permit built on another **MUST** resolve to the union of both: its required SOPs are those of the base plus its own, and its tools are those of the base plus its own. Holding the writing permit therefore carries the reading basis. A chain of permits **MUST NOT** form a cycle. Destructive operations — removing a worktree, recording a snag, deregistering a work item — are carried by neither permit.

---

## The Reading Limit of a Comment

The right to write a comment about a unit of code rests on having **read in full** the unit the comment speaks about. The **scope of the comment** decides which unit that is:

A comment about a method needs the method read in full, a comment about a class needs the class read in full, a comment in the head of a file needs the file read in full.

This limit lies **inside** an existing permit, and it is **not a new permit**. The writing permit says where work may happen; the reading says what a comment may be written about. Neither replaces the other: holding the writing permit for a repository does not entitle a comment about a class that was read in part, and a full reading does not entitle a write outside the permit's location. A keyword search is not a reading; it is declared as a keyword search under the principles of conduct in [./10-spirit.md](/governance/spirit/), and this chapter does not define reading a second time.

---

## Root and Project

Permits exist inside a **project** only. The level of a call is found by ascending from its working directory: the first directory carrying the project registry is a project; a directory carrying the workbench session folder and the projects folder is the workbench root; everything else lies outside the workbench. At the root a closing SOP **MUST** refuse the release, with the reason that the root level carries no permit; outside the workbench the permit layer decides nothing. A project that carries no registry of its own is seen from the root and carries no permit, which is the safe side.

---

## Permits in the Life Cycle of a Unit of Work

A permit is a precondition of the life cycle of a unit of work. The reading basis is required when a unit is generated, when it is built and when it is evaluated; each of those entry points **MUST** name the permit twice, as prose and as a machine-readable mark, and a hook refuses the entry point while its holder has no valid permit. The writing permit is not tied to an entry point: it binds through its tool list at the location where the writing happens.

Per stage of the life cycle — generate, execute, evaluate — a permit names the additional skills that stage needs. The naming is a declaration; it enforces nothing beyond what the entry points and the tool list already enforce.

---

## The Holder and the Three-Valued Check

Destructive rights do not rest on a permit as long as the holder cannot be checked; until then they keep running through deny rules and the user's release. The holder of an identity-bearing or destructive command is checked by comparing the name the command states with the name the harness gave the calling context. The check has four outcomes, and contradiction and absence of a statement **MUST NOT** be folded together:

| Outcome | What lies on the table | Destructive class | Reading, authorising, writing |
|---|---|---|---|
| match | the stated name and the harness name agree | not granted by a permit — the user's release is asked | allowed |
| contradiction | both are present, and they differ | refused | refused |
| no statement | the harness reports no sub-agent, or no harness name is readable | refused by the permit — the user's release is asked | allowed |
| malformed | a command that can carry a name carries none, or the name does not parse | refused | refused |

Folding contradiction into absence of a statement yields a gate that reports green over nothing; folding absence of a statement into contradiction yields a gate that blocks every main session, including the one writer of a memo store that commits on behalf of a worker. A command that has no slot for a name is decided by the harness alone. A check never rewrites the command it judges.

---

## Refused Commands Are Recorded

Every refusal of a permit gate **MUST** be recorded — in warn mode as well as in block mode — in an append-only ledger of the session: the gate, its verdict, its decision, the class of the command, its verb where it has one, and a hash prefix of the command. The ledger **MUST NOT** hold the command text, because a command can carry a secret. Without this record the effect of a gate stays a claim, and the decision to make it sharp has no measurement to stand on.

---

## An Asserted Identity Is Not Proof

An identity that an agent asserts about itself **MUST NOT** be accepted as proof when a permit is checked. A name the agent writes into a commit or a receipt is self-reported; unless it is verified against the agent identifier that the harness assigns, the whole permit model rests on self-disclosure. A permit check therefore compares the claimed identity with the identity the harness records, and a claim without that match counts as unverified.

---

## A Write Onto a Foreign Work Item Is Refused

A write that changes the status of a foreign work item — one held by another order or another agent — **MUST** be refused. A permit is bound to a place, and a work item outside the place of the permit belongs to its holder; setting it to done without disposition and reason records work that was never done. The refusal names the work item, its holder and the permit that would be needed, so that the agent hands the change to the holder instead.

---


## The Question Permit

The orchestrator role holds the right to put a question to the user only once it has met four care rules. The right sits **at the role**, not at the question: how a question has to look is settled by the question interface ([/specification/question-interface/](/specification/question-interface/)), and this section settles who may put it. The two places point at each other and neither repeats the other.

No rule of this kind existed before this section. That is stated as a measurement: a keyword search (not a search by concept) for `sorgfaltsregel`, `zulassungstest`, `frageberechtigung`, `entitled to ask`, `permitted to ask`, `may only ask` and `duty of care`, without regard to case, found 0 hits over 1,782 Markdown files on 2026-09-28.

### The Four Care Rules

The four rules are demanded together, never one instead of another. Each names how its keeping is checked: **computed** from the record, or **read**.

| Rule | Derived from | Check |
|---|---|---|
| The question passes the admission test of the question form: it stands in the `questions-json` block and carries at least two real options in the form `A) text`, a recommendation with its reasoning and the six lifecycle fields | the question interface | computed — the parser checks the form already |
| The carrier block lies above the conversation threshold, measured as the binary completeness of all mandatory sections of the block — a verdict, not a number | the conversation threshold of the block | computed — the completeness of the mandatory sections is measured in one run, without a new tool |
| The measurement the question rests on has run and names its comparison set; a question about something the orchestrator could have measured is not admissible | the marking duty of a measurement | read — that the comparison set is named can be checked, that the number is right cannot |
| The own stock was searched first — the database, the memo system, the existing topics and the answered questions; asking an answered question again is the most expensive fault on this channel | the search duty of the record | computed — the search leaves a trace on the read path |

### The Bookkeeper Establishes Compliance

Whether the rules were kept is established by the bookkeeper ([./05-roles.md](/governance/roles/), *The Bookkeeper*), not by the orchestrator itself and not by the user: a role that checks its own right checks nothing.

### Rejected, Not Discarded

A question put without its care rules met is **rejected, not discarded**. It stays in the stock under its id with the status `open`, carries the missing care step as its blocking reason, and stands with that reason among the held-back questions of the revision preface — the same place the conversation threshold uses for a question it holds back. The way to the release is therefore always named: run the missing measurement, search the stock, lift the block over the threshold. The rejection is recorded in the append-only ledger of *Refused Commands Are Recorded* above, because a question that is rejected again and again is a symptom, not a single case.

### The Duty to Ask Takes Precedence

The permit is read together with the duty to ask of the behavioral guardrails ([/specification/behavioral-guardrails/](/specification/behavioral-guardrails/), C13): below roughly 75 percent of planned implementation the question MUST be asked, and rejecting the intent without a question oversteps the competence of the role. A question that rule demands is never blocked by this permit; the missing care step is done first, with priority, and the question is not suppressed. A care rule that made a mandatory question disappear would only dress the overstepping in a procedure.

### The Worker Boundary

Systemic changes are discussed by the orchestrator with the user, in a defined process. A worker does not attempt a systemic change: it reports the change it sees to its lead, and the change travels upwards from there. The boundary follows the one-way direction of the role groups ([./05-roles.md](/governance/roles/)) — intervention runs downwards, and a right never travels upwards.

---

---
title: "Permit Validity, Renewal and Expiry"

governance_version: "0.1.0"

edit_warning: "This file is auto-generated. Source: governance/0.1.0/draft/spec/04-permit-validity.md."
---


This chapter specifies the life of a permit over time. A permit is renewed like a driving licence and is never valid forever, so that a context that degrades over a long session is met with a fresh reading of what matters. When and how a permit expires, and what an agent is told before it does, is the subject of this chapter.

---

## Scope

- The triggers of an expiry: a number of commands after which a renewal is required, and the events that end a permit at once.
- An advance warning before the expiry, so that an agent learns in time that a renewal is due — for example a fixed number of commands before the role has to be read again.
- Cascade revocation: when a role is reset, every SOP read under it is revoked as well and has to be read again if still needed; a compaction of the context resets all permissions but not the memory of having held them and why.
- Renewal like a driving licence, never valid forever.

---

## Two Triggers

A permit expires on **two** triggers, and on nothing else:

1. **Events.** A compaction of the holder's context and a role reset of the holder end every permit of that holder at once.
2. **A command count.** A permit **MUST** expire once its holder has issued a fixed number of commands since the grant — under a role, since the release of the role (*The Role Carries the Count*). The number is a value with a named source: the permit may carry its own, otherwise a default applies, and every answer about validity states which of the two was used.

A permit carries no overall cap: its validity is bounded by the two triggers alone. The fill level of the context is not a trigger; it cannot be measured from where expiry is computed. Time is not a trigger either.

Renewal is the regular acquisition: the required SOPs are read again and the closing SOP is run again. Renewal starts a new count; nothing extends a running one.

---

## Where Expiry Is Computed

Expiry **MUST** be computed outside the holder. It is computed at the gate that runs before each tool call anyway: the gate counts the holder's tool calls from the transcript the harness keeps of the holder — the holder's own transcript, for a sub-agent its own and not the session's — so no record of its own has to be kept and no call is ever left uncounted by a hook that did not run. Validity is recomputed on every call from the grant and that count; a recorded expiry is information, not the carrier of the state.

The harness writes the transcript asynchronously, so the count can lag behind the calls by a few; against a threshold of hundreds of commands that lag is acceptable. The hook after a call runs only on skill calls, where it records the release of a permit and a role reset; it does not count.

---

## Advance Warning

Before the count runs out, the holder **MUST** be warned on the channel that reaches the agent — not only the user — once a fixed number of commands remains. The warning is descriptive, not commanding: it names the permit, its location, the commands that remain and **every** SOP that expires with it — the SOPs the permit requires and the SOPs the holder read alongside since the grant. The gate gives it on every call inside the warning window, from the same transcript count it decides on, so that it survives a full context; it is recorded once per grant.

---

## The Role Carries the Count

Original wording (German):

> „Dieser Laufzeit angabe sollte aber gesammelt über die höchste ebene durchgeführt werden. Also dem rollen-sop.“

The command count is collected at the highest level, the role. When the holder has loaded a role start SOP, the release of the role after its closing SOP ([./05-roles.md](/governance/roles/), *Two SOPs Per Role*) is the start of the count — before a release, the role reset is — and every permit granted after it **MUST** count from the role reset, not from its own grant: the permits count onto the role. The role uses the default values of the permits.

- **Advance warning.** Once the fixed number of commands remains, the holder **MUST** be warned on the agent's channel that the role expires: the role, the commands that remain and every SOP the holder read since the role reset, together with the renewal — the start SOP again, the required SOPs, the closing SOP. The warning is given on every call inside the window and recorded once per role reset.
- **Expiry.** When the count is used up, the expiry of the role **MUST** revoke the release of the role, every reading and every permit of its holder, the role SOP itself included, with the same scope as a role reset. It is recorded once.

A holder without a role reset keeps the count of each permit from its grant, as above.

*Provenance: the input transcript of the memo that founded this family, line 203, a statement of the user. Origin: user (`author = user`). Evidence level: opinion (`grade = opinion`).*

---

## Cascade Revocation

A role reset — a successful load of a role start SOP; the closing SOP of a role is no reset — **MUST** revoke every reading and every permit of its holder, except the role SOP that triggered it. A reset of the main context revokes for the whole session; a reset of a sub-agent revokes for that sub-agent only. The SOP gates **MUST** honour the revocation: a reading recorded before it no longer counts, and a reading done again after it counts again. A reading in the same second as the revocation counts as revoked — the conservative side.

---

## Catch-Up Rule

A permit acquired long before the work is, at the moment of use, either inside its warning window — the use is allowed, with the warning — or expired. An expired permit **MUST NOT** be extended after the fact and has no grace period; the refusal names the regular way to acquire it as the next step. A call that has already started runs to its end: the gate decides before a call, never in the middle of one.

---

## The Compaction Bracket

A compaction is bracketed by two halves. The front half runs before the compaction: it **MUST** record, for the holder, every permit held at that moment — the permit, its location, the SOPs it requires and the grant it was held under — and mark each of them as expired, together with a revocation of the holder's readings. The front half never blocks the compaction.

The back half is the one path through which context is injected after a compaction. It **MUST** only describe: it names the expired permits, their locations, the SOPs to read and the way to acquire them again, and it grants nothing. A permit is granted again only through its closing SOP; restoring after a compaction means injecting the list again, never a silent re-grant, because the reading the permit stood on is no longer in the context.

If the second half of the bracket does not run, the permit stays expired; it is neither valid nor undetermined.

---

---
title: "Roles and Role Groups"
description: "A **role** sits above the permits. It collects permits and skills, and it holds the one capability a permit never holds: it may create sub-agents. This chapter first states the criterion that makes..."
governance_version: "0.1.0"
spec_file: "05-roles.md"
order: 5
section: "Governance"
normative: true
generated_at: "2026-11-08T20:57:05.189Z"
generated_from: "governance/0.1.0/draft/spec/05-roles.md"
generator: "scripts/generate-docs-payload.mjs"
edit_warning: "This file is auto-generated. Source: governance/0.1.0/draft/spec/05-roles.md."
---


A **role** sits above the permits. It collects permits and skills, and it holds the one capability a permit never holds: it may create sub-agents. This chapter first states the criterion that makes something a role, then fixes **one** role vocabulary with a deterministic table per role, and then cuts the individual roles — orchestrator, lead, bookkeeper and author — together with the worker functions that run below them. The order is deliberate: a word comes first, a role second, its rights third, because a role that cannot be named on every surface cannot carry a right.

---

## The Criterion of a Role

A role is defined by one capability: **only a role creates sub-agents, and only with fewer rights than it holds itself**. Everything else a role carries — knowledge, permits, skills — can also be collected in a permit; the right to create sub-agents cannot. Whatever creates sub-agents is therefore a role, and whatever does not is either a permit or a function that runs inside a role.

By this criterion the **Lead Role** is a role of its own: the lead is the agent that creates worker sub-agents and has them carry out the work. The lead role is not the orchestrator contract role, and it is not a second name for the orchestrator: it is a separate role that runs under that contract role, with a narrower reach and without contact to the user. A lead never becomes an orchestrator by holding more permits, because the difference is not one of knowledge.

The bookkeeper stands outside this chain. It creates no sub-agents and is neither above nor below the orchestrator, the lead or the workers; it watches the procedure rather than the work. The criterion separates the chain roles from the worker functions, and it does not apply to the bookkeeper, whose standing is defined in *The Bookkeeper* below.

---

## Role Vocabulary

There is **one** role vocabulary. Each role has exactly one word, and the word is fixed by the table below; no surface coins a second word for a role that already has one.

| Word | Tier | Area | Booking value | Contract role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `orchestrator` | 1 | rollout | `orchestrator` | `orchestrator` |
| `author` | 1 | research (authoring up to finalization) | `author` | `user` |
| `lead` | 2 | research or rollout | `lead` | `orchestrator` |
| `worker` | 3 | any | `worker` | `worker` |
| `bookkeeper` | standalone | procedure | `bookkeeper` | `worker` |

The word of a role is binding on four surfaces at once — the specification text, the skill text, the stored agent label in the form `<word>:<subject>`, and the terminal output — as the memo family states for its working roles ([/specification/orchestrator-role/](/specification/orchestrator-role/)). Whoever introduces a role serves all four surfaces in one go; a role that is present on fewer than four of them is a role that cannot be booked, and it **MUST NOT** be given rights until it can.

The *Contract role* column names the tool contract a running context executes under ([/spec/harness-registry/](/spec/harness-registry/)). A working role projects onto a contract role; it does not add a contract role of its own.

---

## Two SOPs Per Role

Every role carries **two** SOPs, as [./02-sop-system.md](/governance/sop-system/) requires of every role and permit: the **start SOP** `role-<name>` and the **closing SOP** `role-<name>-close`. A role is a sandwich SOP: start SOP, the required SOPs, closing SOP.

| Role skill | Start SOP | Closing SOP | Required SOPs |
|---|---|---|---|
| author | `role-author` | `role-author-close` | `session-sop`, `workbench-sop`, `memo-sop` |
| planner | `role-planner` | `role-planner-close` | `session-sop`, `workbench-sop`, `memo-sop` |
| orchestrator | `role-orchestrator` | `role-orchestrator-close` | `session-sop`, `workbench-sop`, `memo-sop`, `controlled-language` |
| lead | `role-lead` | `role-lead-close` | `session-sop`, `workbench-sop`, `memo-sop` |
| worker | `role-worker` | `role-worker-close` | `session-sop`, `workbench-sop`, `memo-sop` |
| bookkeeper | `role-bookkeeper` | `role-bookkeeper-close` | `session-sop`, `workbench-sop`, `memo-sop` |

- **The start SOP** says what the role is and which SOPs have to be read for it. Loading it is the **role reset**: every reading and every permit the holder had before is revoked ([./04-permit-validity.md](/governance/permit-validity/)). It **MUST** file its required SOPs twice — as a prose list and as the marked line `<!-- role-requires: … -->` — and both filings **MUST** name the same set.
- **The closing SOP** ends the reading. It **MUST NOT** be executable before every required SOP has been read in the same session: the gate before every tool call reads the marked line of the start SOP and refuses the call of the closing SOP while one of the SOPs it names is unread, and the refusal **MUST** name every missing SOP, so that the agent meets the expected behaviour and not a silent stop. The registry edges (`when: pre` and `when: post`, one per required SOP) carry the same set as the machine-readable twin. Loading the closing SOP is **not** a role reset.
- **The release of the role.** The release is a **named state**, `role-granted`, and it **MUST** arise only from a successful closing SOP after which a hook has judged every required SOP as read; a hook records it, never the holder. A closing SOP with a SOP missing releases nothing and records the refusal with the missing SOPs. The state is shown to the agent on its channel. Today the release carries the state itself and the start of the role's command count; no tool right depends on it yet. The expiry of the role takes the release away.
- **The role carries the count.** The command count of the holder starts at the release of the role — before a release, at the role reset — the permits granted under the role count onto it, an advance warning names the commands that remain and every SOP read since the reset, and the expiry of the role revokes every reading and every permit of the holder ([./04-permit-validity.md](/governance/permit-validity/), *The Role Carries the Count*).
- **The required SOPs per role.** Every role reads the three SOPs of the SOP chain. A role adds an SOP of its own where this chapter names one for it: the orchestrator answers the user in normalised language (*The Answer Duty*), so it also reads `controlled-language`. Knowledge for work at a place — git and node for a repository — is not a role's: it is carried by the permits the work needs (`repo-worker`, `repo-coder`; [./03-permits.md](/governance/permits/)), which normalise that knowledge across roles, so a role does not carry it a second time.
---

## Role Tables

Each role is described by exactly one table with the same seven fields in the same order. The tables are deterministic: two readers who look up the same field of the same role get the same answer, and a field that a role does not fill is written out rather than left away.

The seventh field, *Communication*, names with whom a role communicates and over which path. A role is created only with its communication field filled, and the default is no communication at runtime. Communication between roles is defined, not improvised ([./11-risk-surface.md](/governance/risk-surface/)).

### Role: `orchestrator`

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Word | `orchestrator` |
| Tier | 1 |
| Rights | Creates sub-agents — leads and workers — only with fewer rights than it holds itself; appoints the leads; is the only chain role that holds the communication with the user; holds almost every right and carries the highest quality claim of all roles. It is the only role that lays down a snag in the cross-memo snag store (`memo snag add`) — the last resort, recorded with its creator and counter-cleared by the highest level. |
| Booking value | `orchestrator` |
| Contract role | `orchestrator` |
| Surfaces | spec: this chapter · skill: `role-orchestrator` · stored label: `orchestrator:<subject>` · terminal: the same label |
| Communication | the user, and its leads and workers through defined handover documents |

### Role: `author`

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Word | `author` |
| Tier | 1 |
| Rights | Creates research sub-agents only with fewer rights than it holds itself; writes the authoring tables of a memo; its span ends with the finalization of the memo. |
| Booking value | `author` |
| Contract role | `user` |
| Surfaces | spec: this chapter · skill: `role-author` · stored label: `author:<subject>` · terminal: the same label |
| Communication | the user, and research results as delivered files |

### Role: `lead`

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Word | `lead` |
| Tier | 2 |
| Rights | Creates worker sub-agents only with fewer rights than it holds itself; communicates only with the orchestrator. |
| Booking value | `lead` |
| Contract role | `orchestrator` |
| Surfaces | spec: this chapter · skill: `role-lead` · stored label: `lead:<subject>` · terminal: the same label |
| Communication | the orchestrator only; its workers through order sheets and receipts |

### Role: `worker`

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Word | `worker` |
| Tier | 3 |
| Rights | Creates no sub-agents; carries out one bounded unit of work and writes the proof of its own work. It lays down no snag in the cross-memo snag store; a defect it cannot fix goes back to its lead as a finding. |
| Booking value | `worker` |
| Contract role | `worker` |
| Surfaces | spec: this chapter · skill: `role-worker` · stored label: `worker:<subject>` · terminal: the same label |
| Communication | none at runtime; it delivers its receipt |

### Role: `bookkeeper`

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Word | `bookkeeper` |
| Tier | standalone |
| Rights | Creates no sub-agents; watches the procedure, as described in *The Bookkeeper* below. |
| Booking value | `bookkeeper` |
| Contract role | `worker` |
| Surfaces | spec: this chapter · skill: `role-bookkeeper` · stored label: `bookkeeper:<subject>` · terminal: the same label |
| Communication | none at runtime; it writes referrals into the record |

---

## Worker Functions

Workers are **functions on tier 3, not roles**. They create no sub-agents, so by the criterion above they are not roles; they are the different kinds of bounded work a worker carries out. A function is named in the subject of the stored label, while the booking value stays the one listed here.

| Function | What it does | Booking value |
|---|---|---|
| `prd-generator` | cuts and writes one unit of work from the material it is given | `worker` |
| `prd-builder` | carries out one unit of work and writes the proof of it | `worker` |
| `prd-evaluator` | checks one finished unit of work in a fresh context | `evaluator` |
| `researcher` | researches one subject in depth and delivers the result as a file | `research` |
| `transcriber` | takes a user transcript in, cleans it and checks it | `worker` |
| `finalizer` | runs the readiness checks that close the authoring of a memo | `worker` |
| `planner` | turns a finalized memo into a phase plan and hands it over | `worker` |

The two booking values `evaluator` and `research` are kept: they already exist as stored values and separate the fresh-context checker and the research fan-out from the other workers. The `planner` is a worker function, as in the role tree the system was designed from, and not a head role.

The workers know nothing of each other. A generating worker does not know which worker will build its unit, and a building worker does not know which worker will check it; yet all of them carry **one** common goal, and each of them works autonomously to complete its own part as professionally as possible.

The role information is neutral: what holds equally for generating, building and evaluating a unit is stated once, for all three, and none of the three is told about the other two. The will to carry the work out correctly is conveyed through the structure — through the cut of the unit, the conditions it is checked against, and the proof it must deliver — and not through direct words of encouragement.

---

## The Orchestrator

The orchestrator is the **authorized officer** of the system: like a holder of general commercial power of attorney, it can do almost everything, and therefore it carries the highest quality claim of all roles. Its limits are as clear as its reach. Its rights pass downwards only — every lead and every worker it creates holds fewer rights than it does —, and above it the user always remains the highest authority ([./10-spirit.md](/governance/spirit/)).

Its standing duty is to **keep the machine running** and to prevent blockages: work that has been commissioned has to flow, and a stop that nobody resolves is the orchestrator's failure, not the worker's. Because it is the most powerful agent, it carries the strictest duty to keep its own context clean — the more powerful an agent is, the more it has to guard its context, and this applies to the leads as well, which are in constant communication with their workers.

A memo is a **closed environment**. The orchestrator is obliged to close that environment correctly, so that the memo works as a link in a chain of memos; an orchestrator whose actions break that chain does not act in the spirit of this system. This is a setting by the user, not a derived rule, and it can be changed only by the user.

*Provenance: user statement carried over from an earlier draft that is classified as contaminated. Evidence level: assumption.*

### The Answer Duty

The user speaks freely. The orchestrator is the user's only real counterpart and answers in normalised language: the approved words of the anchor-term register and the rules SR-01 to SR-12 of [controlled-language](/spec/controlled-language/). Hand-overs between roles use the same words; the dictionary view of the register is the list of those words. The user is never asked to speak in this form.

---

## The Lead

The lead is a role between the orchestrator and the workers. It differs from the orchestrator in two ways: it never ascends to the orchestrator, and it has no contact with the user. It differs from a worker in one way: it creates sub-agents, while a worker does not. A lead is appointed by the orchestrator and focuses on carrying out the work it was given.

Research and rollout need differently cut leads, because the work in the two areas follows different rules. A **research lead** works completely and accurately: a document is read in full before it may be quoted, and the strict rules for each part of a revision apply, because the revision is the basis of all later work. A **rollout lead** may use a narrower search, because the information it works on already has a structure that is better suited to a targeted search. The booking value of both is `lead`; the area is carried in the subject of the stored label.

A lead communicates **only with the orchestrator**. It does not address the user, and it does not open a channel to another lead; a question it cannot answer goes to the orchestrator.

---

## The Bookkeeper

The bookkeeper is a **role of its own**. It is responsible for the correctness of the database entries and for the record always showing the current state of the project. It administers the project version history that sits outside the repository folder and sets strategic reset points in it; that history cannot be deleted by any other role and lies outside their reach. And it is responsible for every user input being recorded, because a user intent can only be traced back — and shown to have been the user's view until the end — when every input that formed it was recorded along the way.

The bookkeeper watches the **procedure, not the practical work**. It does not check folders or review results; it checks that the mandatory entries were made and that the procedure was kept, and it intervenes quickly where the procedure was broken, to strengthen the spirit of the system and the efficiency of the work. It stands alone in the role groups, with no edge upwards or downwards to the orchestrator, the lead or the workers.

### The Bookkeeper Is a Calculator

The bookkeeper is a calculator driven by a cadence, not a reader. The orchestrator cannot skip it. It is woken at the breakpoint of the tool-call cadence — the same cadence the session breakpoints are counted at — and not called up by any role. Its one data source is the queue that the one write path fills: every write of every other role leaves one pending item in it, in the same commit as the write itself. When it is woken, the bookkeeper works the queue to its end, including items that arrive while it works. There is no interval and no wake-up per write.

### The Five Surfaces

| Surface | What it calculates | Comparison set |
|---|---|---|
| `carrier-checks` | the carrier checks of the memo | every verdict line of the checks |
| `parity` | the flat stock against the database, axis by axis | the compared rows of each axis; an axis that compared nothing is red |
| `reporting-duty` | the open work items that carry a disposition | all open work items; none open is not measurable |
| `chronicle` | one line of a time line per run, without grading | the memo-level breakpoints since the previous run |
| `user-inputs` | the completeness of the user inputs in the record | the harness session |

The completeness of the user inputs is calculated against the session the user worked in, never against the record's own copy of itself, and it is never green without a comparison: a record can be consistent with itself and still miss what nobody recorded. Every surface names the side it counts from and how much it compared.

### Five Construction Rules

It never blocks and always calculates. Five rules hold the bookkeeper to that, each of them built and tested:

- It uses no lifecycle event that can block.
- A wake-up is not a start.
- Arrival order is a race, so processing is idempotent.
- It does not rely on the parent field of an agent.
- It checks its own carriers before it calculates.

### The Referral

A referral hangs at the block and goes to the lead, not to the worker that caused it and not to the orchestrator. The lead carries the phase and with it the whole block, while a worker works on units smaller than a block; the one who can work a finding off at the block is therefore the lead. A referral has exactly two states, open and resolved, and no way to be deleted. Only the lead resolves it, once, with a note. A phase does not close while a referral is open or a queue item is pending.

### Findings Go Into the Order Sheet

A finding of the bookkeeper goes into the order sheet of the responsible lead, never into a lesson. A lesson is read by whoever looks for one; an order sheet is read by the lead who has to act.

### The Bookkeeper Checks the Question Permit

The bookkeeper establishes whether the orchestrator kept the four care rules of the question permit ([./03-permits.md](/governance/permits/), *The Question Permit*). The orchestrator cannot establish it about itself without turning the permit into a self-assessment, and the user is not the checker of a procedure. Three of the rules the bookkeeper computes over the record: the admission test of the question form, the conversation threshold of the carrier block as a binary verdict, and the search of the own stock as a trace on the read path before the question was put. The fourth it reads: it checks that the measurement names its comparison set, not that its number is right.

### The Blind Spot

The bookkeeper sees what was entered, never what was not entered. A row that nobody wrote leaves nothing to calculate over. The other side is covered by the phase matrix ([/specification/orchestrator-role/](/specification/orchestrator-role/), section *The Phase Matrix*), which holds every order of a running phase against the carriers it has to fill.

### Supervision of the Lead

The bookkeeper supervises the lead. The supervision of the roles is asymmetric: workers are supervised closely, the orchestrator is supervised by the user, and the lead stands between them with much room. The bookkeeper fills that middle tier with two means — the referrals it counts per phase, with their age, and the phase gate it holds. It does not intervene in the work.

### Strategic Version Points

The bookkeeper sets the strategic version points of the project version history. There are four occasions:

- before the rollout begins
- at every phase close
- before the local merge into the main line
- at the landing

The version history lies outside the repository folders, has no remote, and cannot be deleted by any other role; the deletion protection itself is built elsewhere.

### The Orchestrator's Triple Task

The orchestrator carries three tasks at once: the conversation with the user, the working off of the run, and the holding together of the stock. Measured on one memo, 5 of 236 open work items carried a disposition — 2.1 %, with all open work items of the memo as the comparison set. A role that carries three tasks at once does not also supervise the procedure; the supervision of the procedure is the bookkeeper's.

The watch of a running phase is enforced at the turn end of the leading session: while a worktree of a running phase exists and no watch is booked, the turn end is refused with the two commands that arm it. A command-line leaf cannot call the harness tool that creates the timer; what is deterministic is the trigger, not the call. The bookkeeper's finding for an unarmed watch stays the second carrier.

---

## The Author

The author is the role that writes a memo. It takes input in, captures topics and work items, writes the chapters, asks the questions, commissions research and finalizes. It makes its mandatory entries into the record **during** the work, not at its end: an entry made only after the revision is complete has lost the moment it was meant to record, and an authoring step that leaves a carrier empty has to name the reason when authoring ends.

The author is bounded against the orchestrator by time: the author's span runs up to the finalization of a memo, the orchestrator's span starts with the rollout. The two never hold the same memo at the same time.

The author is a role and not a worker function, by the criterion at the top of this chapter: it commissions research and creates research sub-agents for it. The transcriber and the finalizer of the role tree remain worker functions; the author **MAY** hand work to them, as any role may hand work to the functions below it.

---

## Gradient and Horizon

The lower a role sits, the more practical its instructions are. The large idea of the system is shaped from the theoretical into the practical on the way down, until it reaches the worker as a concrete instruction: a worker deep in a problem needs no theory of the system, it needs to know what to do.

The horizon widens on the way up. The worker thinks of carrying out and evaluating its own unit of work. The lead thinks of the work in the context of the other units of its phase, and somewhat beyond. The orchestrator keeps the phases and the current state in view, oversees the whole memo, and sees its own work in the chain of the tasks before and after it.

Each role therefore has a goal horizon of its own: the worker's horizon is its own assignment, the lead's horizon is the phase, the orchestrator's horizon is the memo. A role that does not know the goal of its level cannot judge its own contribution, which is why each role carries the sentence that states where it stands in the system and what it answers for.

*Provenance: user statement carried over from an earlier draft that is classified as contaminated. Evidence level: assumption.*

---

## Equal Standing at the Role Level

The roles stand equal at the role level, not on the plane of the persons or bearers who carry them. The question whether a worker is as important as the architect confuses a role with its bearer: a role is a part of the system's carrying structure, and a bearer is whoever fills it at the moment. The equal standing is a statement about the roles. What a distribution among them looks like follows from it, and is stated in [./10-spirit.md](/governance/spirit/).

The work divides into content and form. Content is basically more work than form — if form outweighed content, the system would be a bureaucratic monster that produces structure and little else. The higher a role stands, the fewer bearers it has, the more theoretical it becomes, and the more its work is about form. Without form there is no structure and no scaling; without workers there is no content for the form to shape. Neither half stands without the other.

The quantities follow from this: one system architect, one or two orchestrators or one per strand, many leads, and still more workers. The architecture only becomes necessary once there are many workers. If the number of workers falls away, the reason for everything above them falls away with it.

The message that reaches each role differs on purpose; that difference is not a breach of the equal standing, as [/specification/internal-vs-external-communication/](/specification/internal-vs-external-communication/) states.

---

## The Tool Duty

Every role receives the tools its work demands. The reason is the weakest link: the chain gives way at its weakest point, so a role without its tools is not a matter of comfort but a risk for the whole system, and it is recorded as a system risk.

The duty is checkable. The measuring rule compares each role against the list of tools its work demands, and a role for which the list is missing or unmet counts as a risk. The comparison set is the five roles of the table in *Role Vocabulary*. A role without its tools is a finding to be named, not a state to be tolerated.

---

## The Asymmetry of Supervision

The supervision of the roles is asymmetric, and this chapter names that as a finding. Workers are supervised closely. The orchestrator is supervised by the user, and the norm text around it is dense: a chapter of its own, a status report at an interval, bundles of questions and a duty to recommend. The lead stands between the two, holds much power, and is supervised in the procedure by no one — the least supervised of the three roles. The bookkeeper fills the middle tier, as the section *Supervision of the Lead* describes; it is not repeated here.

The null finding is stated with its measurement. On 2026-09-28, of 122 chapters, 0 of 122 carried a title for the lead, the worker or the bookkeeper, and exactly 1 of 122 carried a role name, the orchestrator role. The measurement was repeated on 2026-10-12 over the chapters of all five families of this tree: 1 of 132 titles names a single role (the orchestrator role), and none names the lead, the worker or the bookkeeper. The roles now stand together in this chapter. This section builds no new supervision procedure; it names the finding and the means, the bookkeeper.

The warning of the user stays in his words. *Original wording (German):* „Und da müssen wir aufpassen, dass es nicht Elite wird. LEAD.“ In English: the lead must not become an elite.

---

## Role Group Tree

The roles are ordered in three groups, from the top down `orchestrator` > `lead` > `worker`, and one position stands outside that order: the bookkeeper. The table gives every booking value exactly one row; a worker function is booked under the value of its row in *Worker Functions* and has no row of its own.

| Role | Group | Rank | Creates sub-agents |
|---|---|---|---|
| `orchestrator` | `orchestrator` | 3 | yes |
| `author` | — | — | yes |
| `lead` | `lead` | 2 | yes |
| `worker` | `worker` | 1 | no |
| `bookkeeper` | `standalone` | — | no |
| `evaluator` | `worker` | 1 | no |
| `research` | `worker` | 1 | no |

The rank counts upwards — the higher the rank, the higher the group — and so runs opposite to the tier numbers of *Role Vocabulary*. A dash marks a value that is not decided by the role table. The author holds tier 1 beside the orchestrator, but the table assigns it to none of the three groups, so no rule of this chapter places it above or below another role. The one dash with a different reason is the bookkeeper's rank: the standalone position carries no rank by definition.

The tree is not a reporting line. It only orders which role a session may take on and into whose work a role may intervene. A session may carry more than one role, but only downwards: every further role it takes on lies below the one it already holds.

---

## No Ascent

A role is taken on only downwards. An orchestrator may take on the role of a lead; a lead never takes on the role of the orchestrator; a worker takes on no other role. The bookkeeper takes on no role of a group and is taken on by none. A change sideways within the same rank is not a step downwards and is not covered by this rule — a `worker` does not become an `evaluator` by it. A role whose group the role table does not decide takes on no other role and is taken on by none, until the table decides its group.

The machine form is `mayBecome(from, to)` of the role table in the reference implementation. How the rule is enforced when a sub-agent is created is specified elsewhere.

---

## The Lead Owns the Phase

The phase is the granularity of the lead. The lead cuts the units of work of its phase — itself, or through a planner that belongs to the worker group —, distributes the work items so that every worker that generates a unit of work receives exactly that unit's share, and merges at the end of the phase. Whoever writes the cut, the responsibility for it stays with the lead.

The distribution is checkable. The shares of a phase are pairwise disjoint, and together they cover the living stock of the phase. `memo phase shares` computes both and refuses a phase whose shares do not add up; no generating worker starts before that check is green.

---

## The Planner Belongs to the Worker Group

The planner belongs to the worker group. The reason is the criterion of a role: creating sub-agents lifts a role above the worker group, and the planner creates none. It is booked as `worker`, and its function is named in the subject of the stored label.

The placement rests on that criterion, not on a track record. Planning held apart from execution has carried where it concerned the phase plan, and it has not carried where it concerned the cut of the units of work. The booked role `planner` itself has never been applied in a run that went to its end, so there is no evidence for it or against it, in either direction.

---

## Duties Anchored From the Executing Layer

This section gives each duty of the executing roles that so far stood only in the executing layer — in a skill, a template or a test — a normative home with its own identifier. Nine such duties had no anchor in the specification. A role duty that lives only in the executing layer falls out at every re-derivation of that layer, as a positive-control duty once already did; anchored here, it survives the next derivation. Each identifier is a spelled-out English name built from the role, the word duty and the subject, and it is the stable token by which skills and templates cite the duty.

### Worker Duty: Self-Acceptance

**Identifier.** worker-duty-self-acceptance

Before handing in, the worker **MUST** run every machine-checkable acceptance condition of its own order itself, with the same commands that the reviewer runs afterwards. It delivers this self-acceptance as one script: one call yields one table with, per condition, the command, the exit code measured before any pipe, the count with its comparison set, the verdict and the negative case. Every condition carries at least one negative case — a constructed violation that the check must catch, measured red and then reverted without residue. No count is green over an empty set; a comparison set of zero is a finding, never a pass. The verdict `OK` is allowed only when every satisfiable condition is measured green; otherwise the verdict is `PROBLEM` with the red condition named in plain words, and an `OK` without a green measurement of its own is a false statement. The duty sits with the worker because a failure costs it minutes while context, tree and tools are open, whereas the same failure after handing in costs a reviewer, a new order and a second round; the reviewer verifies and does not measure anew.

### Worker Duty: Completion Receipt

**Identifier.** worker-duty-completion-receipt

Every worker **MUST** write its completion receipt after its commit and before it ends. The receipt names the commit and the paths of the result inside that commit; a receipt with the verdict `OK` over files that are not committed is refused. A receipt is never overwritten: a second landing is a new attempt with its own number.

### Worker Duty: The Verdict Carries the Result

**Identifier.** worker-duty-verdict-carries-result

The verdict of a receipt **MUST** carry the result of the work, never the fact that the agent ran; that the agent has run is already shown by the receipt existing. `OK` means that the order is really fulfilled, `PROBLEM` means aborted or an own check red. The opening word of the note and the field say the same, and a contradiction between them is refused when the receipt is written and reported when it is checked.

### Worker Duty: The Base of the Result Paths

**Identifier.** worker-duty-result-base

The receipt **MUST** name the base against which its result paths are resolved — for a rollout worker its own work tree — and store that base in the receipt. The check resolves the paths against the stored base, not against the root of the checker; otherwise the honest worker is blocked and a receipt that points at an untouched project file passes. The base itself must be an existing directory inside the project root, and every named path must be a non-empty regular file inside the base.

### Evaluator Duty: Completion Receipt

**Identifier.** evaluator-duty-completion-receipt

The evaluator **MUST** also write a completion receipt before it ends, and its verdict field carries its judgement: its `PASS` becomes `OK`, its `FAIL` becomes `PROBLEM`. The same binding as for the worker applies, for the same reason: that the evaluator has run is shown by the receipt existing. Without this duty at the evaluator, receipts carried `OK` for having run while their notes opened with `FAIL`.

### Lead Duty: The Slim Worker Type

**Identifier.** lead-duty-slim-worker-type

The lead **MUST** start a rollout worker as the slim agent type: an explicit tool allow-list without the tool that spawns agents, no additional servers, the required skills preloaded and the gate hooks on board. When that agent type is not installed in the environment, this is a finding: the lead records it, continues with the standard type and does not claim to have started a slim worker.

### Lead Duty: Name at Spawn

**Identifier.** lead-duty-name-at-spawn

The lead **MUST** spawn every worker with a name composed of role and subject, in the form `worker:prd-07`, and put the human sense — a short title of the order — into the description. The name is the machine label and the description is for people; free text in the name is not allowed.

### Lead Duty: The Label Line in the Prompt

**Identifier.** lead-duty-label-line

The composed prompt of every worker **MUST** carry the machine-readable label line verbatim, with the value composed for the name at spawn. It is the only join key that the agent itself can write into its artefacts, and the line by which the completion gate recognises the worker. Without it the gate does not recognise the worker and lets it through, because an unlabelled agent is passed on purpose rather than a foreign one being blocked.

### Evaluator Duty: Name at Spawn

**Identifier.** evaluator-duty-name-at-spawn

The lead **MUST** spawn every evaluator in a fresh context, without carry-over from the work it checks, with a name composed of the role `evaluator` and the subject, and with a description that states that the context is fresh.

---

generated_from: "governance/0.1.0/draft/spec/06-subagents.md"
